title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Port Monitors
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Port Monitors
summary: A port monitor is a print subsystem component that the print spooler loads to manage communication with a printer port, and an adversary can register their own so an arbitrary library loads at boot. Registration happens either through the AddMonitor interface, which installs a monitor library normally kept in the system directory, or by writing a fully qualified library path to the Driver value of a subkey under the print monitors registry key. Because spoolsv.exe runs as the local system account, the loaded library executes with system level privileges, so the technique yields both persistence across restarts and privilege escalation in one step. The registry key holds entries for standard monitor types such as the local port monitor, the standard TCP/IP port monitor, the USB monitor, and the WSD port, so a new or renamed subkey with an unusual Driver path is the clearest indicator. Defenders monitor that key for additions, inspect which modules the spooler has loaded, and correlate registry writes with subsequent spooler starts and service behaviour.

beginner.definition: A port monitor is a small program that Windows uses to talk to a printer port. The print service loads these programs when the computer starts. An attacker can register their own monitor so their program is loaded too, with the full rights of the system.
beginner.whyItMatters: The print service runs with very high privileges on Windows. Anything it loads inherits those privileges. That means one registry change can give an attacker both a way to run code and a way to run it as the system itself. Printing looks harmless, so monitoring for printing components is often skipped. The attacker's library also returns after every restart.
howItWorks: Windows keeps a list of port monitors in the registry under the print monitors key.
When the print service starts, it reads that list and loads the library named for each monitor.
A program can add a monitor by calling the AddMonitor interface with a library to install.
Alternatively, an attacker writes a full library path into the Driver value of a new subkey.
The library is then loaded by the print service, which runs as the system account.
Detection looks for new monitor names and for libraries loaded by the print service.
beginner.example: Imagine an office building where the mailroom opens at six each morning. The mailroom follows a list of instructions taped inside its door, one line for each delivery route. Someone adds a line naming an outside courier as a route. Every morning the mailroom rings that courier, who then has the run of the building because the mailroom staff have keys to every floor.
takeaways: Printing components run with system privileges, so they deserve the same attention as services and drivers.
Review the print monitors registry key for unexpected subkeys and unusual library paths.
Check which libraries the print service loads, not just which printers are installed.

objectives: Explain what a port monitor is and how the print service loads it.
Identify the registry location that lists port monitors and the standard monitor types it normally holds.
Describe how the AddMonitor interface installs a monitor library and why system privileges result.
Detect unauthorized port monitors using registry monitoring and loaded module inspection.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from print processor abuse in the same subsystem.
Outline containment steps that remove a malicious monitor and its library.
